title: President explains tourism campaign delay | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 17 October 2026 00:00
-     - 22

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake

- Pic by Lasantha Kumara

By Charumini de Silva

Sri Lanka’s long-awaited global tourism promotion campaign remains stalled by shortcomings in the Government’s procurement framework, with President Anura Kumara Dissanayake acknowledging that existing procedures are ill-suited to purchasing creative ideas and marketing expertise.

Speaking at the inauguration of the Sri Lanka Economic and Investment Summit 2026 on Monetary (12), he said the Sri Lanka Tourism Promotion Bureau (SLTPB) had been attempting to advance the promotional initiative for around 18 months, but the process had yet to move forward, highlighting how administrative bottlenecks continue to impede a critical investment in the country’s tourism competitiveness.

“How do we purchase a promotional plan? According to our procurement methodology, a desk can be purchased. However, what is a promotional publicity program? It is an idea and how do we buy an idea?” he asked.

Dissanayake pointed out that procurement procedures developed primarily for purchasing physical goods were inadequate for evaluating creative services, where selecting the best proposal requires different assessment criteria.

The delay comes as Sri Lanka seeks to strengthen international visibility and attract more visitors amid intensifying competition among regional destinations. A sustained global campaign has been viewed by industry stakeholders as critical, particularly as the country has gone for over 15 years without a sustained global tourism promotion campaign, despite having funds available for destination marketing to improving awareness, diversifying source markets and supporting higher tourism earnings.

The President said the SLTPB is expected to call tenders in January, while a smaller-scale promotional project had already commenced in five countries.

In August, SLTPB officials unveiled a detailed promotional blueprint envisaging an immediate Rs. 1.5 billion interim digital and public relations campaign from August 2026 to April 2027 across six key source markets. That plan was to be followed by the much larger Rs. 5 billion global branding campaign, scheduled to commence in March 2027 and continue through February 2029 (https://www.ft.lk/top-story/Rs--1-5-b-interim-tourism-campaign-kicks-off-ahead-of-global-brand-push/26-796239).

On 31 August, just days after Sri Lanka Tourism unveiled a roadmap envisaging the launch of its global branding campaign, Tourism Deputy Minister Prof. Ruwan Ranasinghe said the long-awaited global destination marketing campaign is set to face a further delay of nearly one year, as the Government was prioritising another consultancy exercise before the final campaign can be awarded https://www.ft.lk/front-page/Another-year-s-wait-for-Sri-Lanka-s-global-tourism-campaign/44-796622#) 

Dissanayake linked the tourism marketing delay to a broader problem in public-sector administration, arguing that rules introduced over time to prevent corruption had created procedures that could obstruct the timely execution of projects.

“There was a mindset in our country that the State machinery is always engaged in corruption,” he said, adding that successive laws and procedures intended to address the problem had reached a point where tasks could not be carried out swiftly.

He said the traditional procurement system was designed largely around purchasing goods, whereas modern public-sector requirements increasingly involved software, services and solutions that could not be assessed through conventional purchasing methods.

“We have identified several specialised and emerging fields requiring new procurement procedures,” he added.

The President also pointed to delays caused by the sequencing of procurement and Budget approvals. “Previously, procurement processes generally began only after the Budget was passed and funds were formally allocated, often pushing the completion of procurement activities to August or September. Now, the Government has addressed this constraint by allowing the Treasury Secretary to certify the availability of funds, enabling procurement preparations to move forward earlier,” he disclosed.

He also said the Government was considering a proposal from tourism industry businesses to reward performance through payments linked to incremental visitor arrivals.

Under the proposed arrangement, funds would be allocated in the next Budget for the Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority (SLTDA) to pay participating businesses if they brought in a higher number of tourists than the target or benchmark for the current year.

The proposal signals a possible shift towards results-based tourism marketing, but details of the baseline, verification mechanism and payment structure were not outlined.

title: Vehicle registrations up 18% in Sept. on two-wheeler rebound | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 17 October 2026 00:00
-     - 15

Vehicle registrations rose 18% month-on-month to 54,214 units in September from 45,811 in August, driven mainly by a rebound in two-wheelers and three-wheelers, JB Securities said. Registrations rose across most major categories, though volumes remained below levels recorded earlier in 2026.

Two-wheelers accounted for the bulk of the increase, rising to 38,747 units from 33,498. Of these, 38,178 were brand-new. TVS led overall for the second consecutive month with 8,684 units, ahead of Bajaj with 8,035 and Honda with 7,673. Bajaj still led brand-new motorcycles with 7,821 units, while Honda led scooters with 7,532, ahead of TVS with 6,668. Financing accounted for 54.4% of two-wheeler registrations.

Three-wheeler registrations rose 37.3% to 5,375 from 3,914. Bajaj dominated the passenger segment with 4,278 units, or 82.2%, followed by TVS with 660 and Piaggio with 166. Cargo three-wheelers added 171 units, led by Piaggio with 126.

Motor car registrations rose to 3,414 from 2,609, with pre-owned cars accounting for most of the gain. Brand-new registrations edged up to 685 from 631, led by BYD with 338 units, almost all ATTO 1s. Pre-owned registrations rose to 2,729 from 1,978, led by Suzuki with 946 units, of which 770 were WagonRs, and Toyota with 683. Small cars below 1,000 cc accounted for 96.5% of brand-new and 98.1% of pre-owned registrations. Financing accounted for 47% of all car purchases.

SUV and crossover registrations increased to 3,941 from 3,226, comprising 1,633 brand-new and 2,308 pre-owned units. Toyota led with 1,357 units, including 1,032 Raizes, followed by Honda with 753, almost all Vezels, and Suzuki with 394, mostly Fronx models. Among Chinese brands, Jetour recorded 289 units and BYD 245. Premium vehicle registrations remained marginal at 77 units, up from 66.

Electric vehicle registrations rose to 6,048 from 5,084, with electric two-wheelers accounting for 5,030 units, led by Yadea with 2,067. Electric motor cars totalled 495 units. The financing share for EVs was 40.1%. JB Securities said this suggests a substantial share of purchases were made without financing, or that dealers registered vehicles before final sale. Hybrid registrations rose to 2,168 from 1,942, almost entirely SUVs and crossovers, led by Toyota and Honda.

Commercial vehicle trends were mixed. Medium-truck registrations rose to 386 units, with Isuzu holding a 77% share, while pickups increased to 361, led by Mahindra. Toyota recorded 116 pickups, including 72 Land Cruiser pickups attributed to the wildlife department. Heavy-truck registrations slipped to 218 from 230, and buses fell to 235 from 271. However, financing penetration for buses rose sharply to 69.8% from 40.6%.

Agricultural machinery also picked up. Large-tractor registrations doubled to 273 from 136, though they remained below June’s 353. Financing penetration in that segment rose to 78.8%, which JB Securities said underlines continued reliance on credit for agricultural machinery.

By origin, Indian imports rose to 36,495 units from 30,669, dominated by 29,308 two-wheelers and 5,299 three-wheelers. Japanese imports increased to 5,930 from 4,735, concentrated in compact cars and SUVs. Locally assembled registrations rose to about 4,999 from around 4,324, of which 4,595 were two-wheelers.

JB Securities said the continued dominance of small cars, small crossovers and two-wheelers highlights the importance of affordability in the market. While the broad-based rise points to a recovery in demand, it said sustainability will depend on household purchasing power, access to credit and the cost of vehicle imports.

title: Rs. 400 b renewable energy pipeline at risk without bankable deals, faster approvals: Expert | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 17 October 2026 00:00
-     - 14

WindForce PLC Managing Director Manjula Perera

—Pic by Ruwan Walpola

Sri Lanka’s plan to attract around Rs. 400 billion in renewable energy and battery storage investment over the next three years could fall short, unless the Government addresses weak power purchase agreements, rupee tariffs, lengthy approval processes and delays in project execution, WindForce PLC Managing Director Manjula Perera warned.

Speaking during a panel discussion at the Sri Lanka Economic and Investment Summit 2026, he said the National System Operator’s (NSO) interim plan for 2027–2029 envisaged adding around 1,400 MW of solar power and 1,000 MW of battery energy storage, creating a substantial pipeline of investment opportunities.

However, he cautioned that the scale of the investment required would exceed the capacity of local investors alone, making foreign capital essential at a time when the sector remained constrained by regulatory and contractual shortcomings.

“Even though the opportunity is there, for the local investors, this is too much on the plate. Then the direct funding investment should come into the country,” he said.

Perera identified three major obstacles to attracting foreign investment, which include; power purchase agreements (PPA) that are not sufficiently bankable, the use of rupee-denominated tariffs for large-scale projects, and a cumbersome approval process requiring over 17 approvals for renewable energy developments.

“A Sri Lankan developer might be able to absorb the time and costs involved, but the same delays could discourage international investors comparing opportunities across markets,” he stressed.

Perera also questioned whether a shift towards competitive tendering, as proposed by President Anura Kumara Dissanayake, would deliver the intended benefits without parallel reforms to land allocation, approvals and contracting.

He said Sri Lanka’s renewable energy industry had largely developed under a feed-in tariff system, while the country had undertaken only three major large-scale tender exercises to date. 

Citing WindForce’s 100 MW solar project at Siyambalanduwa, awarded in 2022, Perera said the Government took around 1.5 years to hand over the required land. “The project was expected to be commissioned by July 2027, but the process from award to commissioning spanned five years,” he added.

He said two 50 MW wind projects at Mullikulam, awarded to WindForce and Vidulanka in February 2026, also illustrated the problem. At the moment, the draft PPA is still with the Attorney General’s Department, while land-related issues remain unresolved.

“On paper, tenders are very good. We will get lower prices, but we have to decide what we want to achieve,” he said, noting that the priority should be to accelerate renewable capacity while reducing dependence on costly thermal power.

Perera said Sri Lanka’s electricity cost structure demonstrated why replacing expensive thermal generation should be a priority.

Noting that renewables accounted for around 54% of electricity generation, he said the remaining share from thermal sources, including diesel-fired plants, accounted for a disproportionately high share of generation costs.

He said thermal generation represented around 46% of electricity supply, but over 71% of the generation costs. Within that mix, diesel-fired generation accounted for around 14% of supply, while contributing around 40% of costs.

He put the average cost of diesel-generated electricity at Rs. 94 per kilowatt-hour, pointing out that reducing reliance on such generation was essential to bringing down the cost burden on consumers.

Perera insisted that these figures reinforce the need to focus on the speed at which cheaper renewable power could be added to the grid, rather than concentrating solely on the tariff secured at the tender stage.

He also said advances in battery storage had created new opportunities to integrate more solar and wind power, while improving grid stability.

“Previously, the high cost of storage meant large thermal power plants had to remain operational to provide system stability and spinning reserve capacity. Battery technology, including grid-forming capabilities, was increasingly able to meet those requirements,” he said.

He welcomed the Government’s battery storage tender program, referring to projects of 160 MW, 250 MW and a further 150 MW. The first 160 MW tranche was at the commissioning stage, while the 250 MW tranche was expected to follow, with the remaining 150 MW to be awarded soon.

Perera called for a stronger national electricity policy and more commercially capable institutions following the unbundling of the Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB).

Despite describing the Electricity Act as a positive development, he opined that the country’s electricity policy needed to be strengthened, noting it appeared to have been formulated in haste.

He also warned that restructuring the CEB into separate entities would not deliver the desired results unless those institutions had adequate human resources and the commercial capabilities required to operate effectively.

“If they are to run like private companies, we see a huge lack of human resources,” he said, calling for the recruitment and development of personnel with private-sector experience and commercial thinking.

Otherwise, he cautioned, the restructuring could simply reproduce existing institutional weaknesses across several successor organisations.

title: High Grown tea output sinks to 34-year low in September | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 17 October 2026 00:00
-     - 10

Sri Lanka’s tea production fell by nearly 9% year-on-year in September to 20.2 MnKg, from 22.1 MnKg a year earlier, as excessive rainfall and poor growing conditions dragged High Grown output down to its lowest level in 34 years, Asia Siyaka Commodities PLC said, citing preliminary data from the Sri Lanka Tea Board.

High Grown production in September stood at 3.49 MnKg, the lowest since 1992, when output was a similar 3.5 MnKg. Asia Siyaka noted that while the 1992 slump was driven by a severe El Niño drought, this year’s decline stemmed from the opposite extreme, with heavy rain and unfavourable weather hampering production.

Mid Grown production also weakened, falling 25% from 4.1 MnKg in September 2025 to 3.09 MnKg, its lowest level since 2023. Low Grown production, however, fared relatively better, rising by 4.8% year-on-year to 13.6 MnKg.

Cumulative production for the January to September period amounted to 192.6 MnKg, a 3% decline from 199 MnKg recorded in the corresponding period of 2025.

All three elevations recorded lower cumulative output than in 2025. Combined High Grown and Mid Grown production fell by approximately 4 MnKg, while Low Grown production declined by around 2 MnKg year-on-year, Asia Siyaka said.

title: US invests $ 17 m to digitalise Colombo Port | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 17 October 2026 00:00
-     - 12

US Ambassador Eric Meyer (left) with SLPA Chairman Dr. Parakrama Dissanayake at the Colombo Port in the presence of Ports and Civil Aviation Minister Anura Karunathilaka (extreme left)

The US will provide $ 17 million to digitise operations at the Port of Colombo, in partnership with the Sri Lanka Ports Authority (SLPA), aiming to cut shipping delays and costs at one of South Asia’s busiest transshipment hubs, the US Embassy in Colombo said yesterday.

The funds will help the SLPA develop two connected digital systems, the Maritime Single Window and the Port Community System. The systems will allow shipping companies, Customs, immigration authorities, port operators and businesses to share information electronically through a single platform, replacing paper-based and disconnected processes that slow down cargo clearance.

An implementing partner will be selected through an open, competitive process, with the Embassy noting that the project will create opportunities for American technology firms to supply the hardware, software and technical expertise required.

The Port of Colombo handles an estimated $ 30 billion in US-related cargo annually. US Ambassador to Sri Lanka Eric Meyer said more than half a million containers of US inbound and outbound cargo move through the port each year.

“When goods move faster and shipping costs come down, American companies are better positioned to compete and American consumers save money. This $ 17 million investment will strengthen the supply chains our economies depend on and support commercial opportunities for American technology companies,” Meyer said.

The Embassy said modern digital infrastructure would be essential as Sri Lanka expands port capacity, to manage higher cargo volumes, reduce vessel turnaround times and keep Colombo competitive as a regional maritime hub.

Ports and Civil Aviation Minister Anura Karunathilaka said Colombo’s future as a regional hub depended not only on expanding physical infrastructure but also on modernising how the port operates. “This project will help Sri Lanka improve trade facilitation, attract business and strengthen our connections to international markets,” he said.

SLPA Chairman Dr. Parakrama Dissanayake said the systems would link the many agencies and businesses involved in port operations. “These new digital systems will help us reduce unnecessary delays and provide more predictable and efficient services to shipping lines and customers,” he said.

In a post on X, Meyer said the platforms would bring shipping companies, Government agencies, port operators and businesses onto a shared digital network, adding that the project would accelerate Sri Lanka’s port modernisation and strengthen US supply chains.

title: Tourist arrivals up 3% in 1H of October | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 17 October 2026 00:00
-     - 13

Sri Lanka welcomed 77,868 tourists in the first 15 days of October 2026, a 3% year-on-year (YoY) increase, but cumulative arrivals for the year remain 1.31% below 2025 levels at just over 1.77 million.

As per the latest figures released, the year-to-date (YTD) figure leaves the country about 30,000 arrivals short of the 1.8 million mark. At the current pace it should be crossed around 21 to 22 October. Based on the reported decline, arrivals at the same point last year were roughly 1.79 million, a gap of about 23,000 visitors.

Average daily arrivals rose to 5,191 in the first half of October, up from 5,044 in the same period last year, an increase of about 147 visitors a day, or 2.9%. 

Within the month, the first week registered 35,786 arrivals and the second week 35,400 and arrivals on 15 October alone reached 6,682, about 29% above the fortnight’s daily average, as the traditionally strong final quarter begins.

India remained the largest source market, sending 29,323 visitors, or 37.7% of arrivals, up 39.8% from 20,982 a year earlier. That 8,341-visitor increase is larger than the entire net gain of about 2,200 for the fortnight. Excluding India, arrivals fell by roughly 11%, from about 54,700 to 48,500.

The other leading markets included China with 5,988 travellers (7.7%), down 7.2% from 6,450; the UK with 5,291 (6.8%), down 11.7% from 5,993; Australia with 4,187 (5.4%), up 14.2% from 3,666 and Germany with 3,644 (4.7%), down 22.3% from 4,689 visitors. 

The top five markets together contributed 48,433 arrivals, or 62.2% of the total, up 15.9% from 41,780 a year earlier. All other markets combined fell about 13%, from roughly 33,900 to 29,400.

On a YTD basis, India has sent 466,737 visitors (about 26% of arrivals), up 17.8% from 396,274 tourists in the same period last year. Australia followed the same direction, with 91,176 arrivals against 81,046, up 12.5%.

However, the traditional Western markets remained softer with the UK sending 166,018 (9%), down  

1.1% YoY from 167,886 in 2025, China with 118,538 (7%), down 5.9% YoY from 125,950, Germany with 100,922 (6%), down 9.6% YoY from 111,677.

The softness in long-haul markets comes against the backdrop of escalated Middle East tensions, which have disrupted air transport with the closure of several airports and airspace. Many European travellers reach Sri Lanka through Gulf hub carriers, and the closures have now forced longer re-routings, reduced connectivity and pushed up airfares and operating costs. Security concerns have added to travellers’ hesitation and the impact is visible in the data. 

Sri Lanka had recorded 1.88 million arrivals by the end of October 2018, meaning about 110,000 more visitors are needed to match that level. At the current daily average, the remaining 16 days of October would add roughly 83,000, bringing the total to about 1.85 million, still around 27,000 short.

The sector now enters its traditionally important winter period. In early September, the SLTDA revised its 2026 projections, citing the continuing impact of the Middle East conflict, higher energy costs and wider uncertainty over international travel.

The revised scenarios place full-year arrivals between 2,377,370 and 2,603,311. The lower figure is only about 17,000 (0.7%) above the 2.36 million record set in 2025, while the upper figure is about 10% higher. Even the upper scenario falls nearly 400,000 short of the original 3 million target, reaching about 87% of it. The lower scenario reaches about 79%.

Reaching those figures will require a sharp acceleration. Roughly 607,000 arrivals (about 7,900 a day) are needed over the remaining 77 days of the year for the lower scenario, and about 833,000 (about 10,800 a day) for the upper. Last year, the same period delivered an estimated 567,000 arrivals, or about 7,350 a day. The lower scenario therefore requires about 7% more than last year’s year-end surge, and the upper one nearly 47% more.

Analysts say the challenge is shifting from generating higher arrival volumes to maximising the value of the winter season, particularly as growth depends heavily on a single market.

title: Chrysalis marks decade of catalysing inclusive change across Sri Lanka | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 17 October 2026 00:00
-     - 11

Chrysalis has completed ten years of working alongside women, youth, and communities across Sri Lanka, a decade measured not just in numbers, but in trust earned, one community at a time.

Founded in 2016, Chrysalis has grown from a locally rooted initiative into an organisation working across inclusive growth, with women and youth at the centre, alongside climate resilience, peacebuilding and inclusive governance. Today, that work spans 18 districts across Sri Lanka and four islands in the Maldives through 92 projects, delivered with 43 donors and 23 partners, reaching 330,000 people directly, with ripple effects extending to a further 11.3 million lives across Sri Lanka. Its guiding belief has stayed constant throughout: lasting change happens when communities, institutions, businesses and development partners choose to build it together. That impact was recognised in 2026, when the Industry and Entrepreneurship Ministr named Chrysalis a key factor in Sri Lanka’s MSME ecosystem.

“Ten years is a milestone, but it is not the destination,” said Chrysalis CEO Ashika Gunasena. “What matters to us is what we have learned along the way, the relationships we have built, and the lives and communities that have shaped our work. I’ve been fortunate to share this journey with a team that continues to bring so much heart, commitment and capability to what we do.”

Alongside its core programmatic work, Chrysalis has built a portfolio of ventures - Chrysalis Advisory Services, Sri Lanka Less Travelled, Made by Her and The HIVE connecting communities and entrepreneurs to markets, expertise and opportunity, and extending impact beyond traditional program delivery. 

The anniversary milestone was marked on 3 September 2026 at the Galle Face Hotel, bringing together development partners, donors, government representatives, diplomatic missions and INGOs who have shaped the organisation’s journey. Guests were taken through “10 Milestones: The Chrysalis Journey,” an immersive retelling of the decade through the voices of the Chrysalis team, alongside a screening of winning films from Third Act: Reframing HER Narratives, celebrating women’s voices and perspectives.

The evening also marked a new chapter: the launch of Chrysalis’ new website, chrysaliscatalyz.com — a single home for the organisation’s programs, ventures and vision, and a platform built for the decade ahead.

“For 10 years, Chrysalis has shown what becomes possible when women, young people and communities are trusted to lead their own change. On behalf of the Board, I thank everyone who has walked this journey with us. Our next chapter is about deepening that trust, widening our reach and building a more inclusive and sustainable Sri Lanka together,” said Chrysalis Chair of the Board of Directors Tamara Bernard.

This journey has been made possible by our diverse and experienced team, and by the trust and partnership of our donors, partners and communities. We remain committed to transparency, accountability and strong financial and support systems as we continue this work.

title: ISMM to host National Supply Chain Day 2026 and National Supply Chain Excellence Awards | Daily FT

The Institute of Supply and Materials Management (ISMM) will lead the celebrations of National Supply Chain Day on 24 October 2026, marking a significant milestone in the recognition and advancement of Supply Chain Management (SCM) in Sri Lanka.

In collaboration with the Industry Ministry, ISMM will organise the National Supply Chain Day Celebrations on 24 October at Monarch Imperial, Sri Jayewardenepura Kotte. The program will feature a full-day seminar, the National Supply Chain Excellence Awards 2026, and ISMM’s 54th Anniversary Banquet Dinner.

Established on 24 October 1972, ISMM has played a pioneering role in developing competent supply chain professionals in Sri Lanka for more than 53 years. Recognising the national and global importance of SCM, and its contribution to economic growth and competitiveness, the Government of Sri Lanka, following recommendations submitted by ISMM and subsequent Cabinet approval, has declared 24 October as National Supply Chain Day.

ISMM is the only professional body in Sri Lanka established by an Act of Parliament (Act No. 3 of 1981) with a mandate to promote and conduct training in Supply Chain Management. The national recognition acknowledges the Institute’s longstanding contribution to professional development and underscores the strategic importance of supply chains to Sri Lanka’s economic progress.

The seminar will take place from 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. under the theme “Geopolitics, Technology, and the Future of Global Supply Chains.” It will bring together local and international supply chain leaders, industry experts and professionals to discuss emerging trends, best practices, technological innovations and the evolving dynamics of global supply chains.

The Government’s recognition provides an official platform to highlight the strategic role of supply chains in national economic development, business resilience and international competitiveness.

CHEC Port City Colombo Ltd., and the Department of Town and Country Planning of the University of Moratuwa have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to strengthen collaboration between academia and industry in urban development, urban informatics, research, innovation and talent development.

Signed on 29 September 2026 at the University of Moratuwa, the agreement will create opportunities for students and academics to engage more closely with the development of Port City Colombo and its planning and development process.

A key focus of the partnership will be student development. The agreement provides for structured internships, industry exposure, academic projects and skills development, with opportunities for longer-term engagement through initiatives such as career fairs involving Port City Colombo-registered entities.

“As a master developer, we see value in working closely with universities because urban development is not something that happens in isolation. We see this as a partnership where both sides have something to gain. Students and academics gain closer access to a major urban development and the practical aspects that come with it, while Port City Colombo gets the benefit of working with people who are researching and thinking about the future of cities. That kind of exchange is something we want to develop further with the University of Moratuwa across all disciplines, as we build Port City Colombo as a platform to further expose Sri Lankan talent to the world,” said CHEC Port City Colombo Ltd., Managing Director Xiong Hongfeng.

The agreement builds on an existing relationship between Port City Colombo and the Department of Town and Country Planning, including previous student engagement through successful initiatives such as the Smart City Ideathon. The initiative gave students an opportunity to engage with urban development challenges related to Port City Colombo. The new agreement broadens this relationship into a more structured programme of research, academic exchange, innovation and industry engagement.

Building on this foundation, the two parties will explore opportunities for applied research and innovation in areas including urban informatics and smart city development. Student and faculty projects may be aligned with emerging urban challenges and areas relevant to Port City Colombo’s development. 

“At a time when Sri Lanka is seeking new pathways towards smarter urban development, this partnership offers a timely opportunity to explore approaches that are not only technologically advanced but also grounded in our local needs, priorities and urban realities. By connecting urban informatics and planning with practical development experience, we hope to generate contextually relevant knowledge and innovative solutions that can inform the future development of cities across Sri Lanka,” University of Moratuwa Department of Town and Country Planning Head Dr. Rizvi Noordeen.

The agreement also provides a foundation for broader collaboration between Port City Colombo and the University of Moratuwa in the future. This could extend beyond the Department of Town and Country Planning to create opportunities for students across the University to upskill, gain industry exposure and engage with international companies operating within Port City Colombo. Such opportunities can give Sri Lankan students greater access to international business and professional experience without having to look outside the country to gain that exposure.

For Port City Colombo, the partnership reflects a broader ambition for the development to function as more than a collection of buildings and infrastructure. As a new city takes shape, its long-term value will also depend on the businesses, institutions, knowledge and innovation that develop within it. The partnership with the University of Moratuwa is one of the ways Port City Colombo is building those connections as the development continues to grow.

title: Shadow economy, 5km blind spot, and unseen cost of inclusion | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 17 October 2026 00:00
-     - 11

Until financial literacy precedes financial inclusion—and until the State provides robust legal shields against predatory asset-stripping—the gates of the formal financial system will remain a fortress that excludes the needy while facilitating the schemer

Introduction: Paradox of the paved corridor

In the opening framing of Dr. W.A. Wijewardena’s Daily FT column, “Alarming case of financial illiteracy amidst drive for financial inclusiveness and literacy,” a stark reality is laid before policymakers: bringing uneducated, unprepared consumers into the formal financial system without equipping them with the intellectual shield of financial literacy is the exact equivalent of handing a high-powered vehicle to an untrained driver.

Yet, when we trace this dilemma from macroeconomic theory down to the asphalt of Sri Lanka’s commercial hubs, the plot thickens. The crisis is not merely that formal financial institutions are thrusting complex credit instruments onto unprepared citizens; the deeper crisis is that a massive, breathing, functioning parallel economy operates entirely outside the perimeter of formal banking—even within literal sight of Central Bank headquarters.

To fully grasp the anatomy of this financial disconnect, we must examine five critical structural observations. Together, these insights expose why financial inclusion without structural literacy and grassroots institutional reform remains an elusive illusion.

I. Five core pillars of financial literacy: Missing foundation

At the genesis of any sound economic policy lies an assumption: that the average citizen understands the basic mechanics of money. The framework we must uphold dismantles this comforting fiction. It defines financial literacy not as an innate trait, but as “the possession of the knowledge, skills, and confidence to make responsible financial decisions and manage personal money effectively.”

In this assessment, true financial literacy rests on five interdependent pillars that are systematically neglected in both standard school curricula and public awareness campaigns. Interestingly, 1. Earning (tracking gross vs. net pay and negotiating compensation), 2. Budgeting (living within means and separating needs from wants), 3. Saving and Investing (building reserves and leveraging compound interest), 4. Borrowing and Debt (managing credit, interest rates, and credit scores) 5. Protecting Assets (guarding against fraud, predatory loans, and risk). 

When these pillars are absent, individuals cannot evaluate the true cost of credit. They see only nominal amounts of immediate cash, remaining entirely blind to compounding interest, hidden fees, and collateral traps. Without this foundational instruction, every push for financial inclusion simply expands the hunting ground for predatory lenders.

II. 5km paradox: Colombo’s unbanked thousands

The prevailing myth among urban planners and monetary authorities is that geographical proximity equals financial integration. If a bank branch sits down the street, the population surrounding it is assumed to be banked.

A startling revelation uncovered during a 2024 urban development initiative shattered this assumption: more than 10,000 families in the City of Colombo, who have benefited from all of our country’s financial systems, do not possess a single bank account (DN, 23.04.24).

Consider the gravity of this paradox. Within a five-kilometer radius of major bank headquarters in central Colombo—surrounded by glass-fronted commercial towers, digital payment gateways, and international trade desks—over 10,000 families operate entirely outside the formal banking system.

Similarly, across the rest of the island, commercial banks mirror real estate “Ribbon Development,” clustering rigidly along main arterial highways to chase high-yield, low-risk commercial transactions. Meanwhile, interior settlements, urban housing schemes, and marginalised communities remain untouched by genuine institutional outreach. The banks are present; the access is absent.

III. Shadow economy: Seettu, Ukas, and Rs. 20 billion micro-debt trap

Because formal institutions erect towering bureaucratic walls, rigid documentation rules, and steep collateral demands, everyday citizens have constructed a vibrant, highly efficient shadow economy. A significant share of national economic activity is driven by women operating through traditional micro-finance mechanisms through Seettu and Ukas.

Seettu (ROSCAs), is Rotating Savings and Credit Associations, where peer trust replaces legal contracts, enabling members to pool capital and access lump sums instantly without interest or paperwork.

Ukas (Pawning), is short-term collateralised borrowing against jewellery and family gold. However, a massive share of pawning transactions occurs entirely outside formal oversight, recorded only if and when desperation pushes borrowers into licensed centres.

Beneath this informal resilience lies an unmonitored debt crisis. A report in 2024 by a Standing Committee of Parliament pointed to a staggering statistic: around 200,000 families are burdened by an estimated Rs. 20 billion in micro-debt, predominantly held with informal micro-creditors and unregulated grassroots networks.

Despite legal safeguards like Article 4 and 5 of the People’s Bank Act tasking State-backed institutions with supervising rural and community credit expansion, these massive liabilities remain unrecorded in macroeconomic ledgers—operating as a breeding ground for systemic default and asset dispossession.

IV. Digital precipice: Scammers, schemers, and ICT illiterate

Compounding traditional financial exclusion is the modern digital revolution. We must recognise that financial illiteracy is no longer confined to the traditional urban and rural poor; it has metastasised across the digital divide.

Financial illiteracy is sparse among both urban and rural poor, but is now expanding rapidly among the ICT-illiterate, who make up easily over 50% of the population. This strangely includes well-qualified senior citizens. Furthermore, school dropouts around Ordinary Levels (O/Ls) account for nearly half the student population; they too find financial literacy difficult if they are not ICT-literate. Standing above them all are “scammers and schemers” operating across both digital and analog mediums.

This creates a two-pronged threat matrix that existing regulatory bodies are ill-equipped to handle:

The Tactical Scammer, relies on direct deceit, fake identities, and false promises via low-friction digital vectors (SMS phishing, WhatsApp links, spoofed phone calls) to trick citizens into voluntarily transferring funds or handing over account access.

The Systematic Schemer, architects broader institutional-scale operations—such as multi-level marketing traps, speculative timber investment rings, and sophisticated Ponzi schemes—that extract capital across entire communities before regulators notice.

When regulatory bodies freeze like “deer caught in headlights”—failing to implement the provided administrative “dentures” to enforce swift consumer protection—vulnerable citizens fall prey. For decades, the Central Bank of Sri Lanka operated without the robust legislative teeth required to regulate monetary responsibilities across the informal fringe. Even when new statutes pass, enforcement lags woefully behind the velocity of cyber fraud.

V. Women’s resilience vs. institutional failure

Perhaps the most profound takeaway is the gendered dichotomy of economic survival.

While formal commercial banks routinely reject low-income women due to a lack of formal pay slips or titled land deeds, these exact women prove to be far more advanced and effective within their own community banking systems. Through Seettu, modern Installment-based or Cooperative models, women maintain disciplined repayment schedules and capital allocation based entirely on social cohesion and mutual accountability.

When formal credit fails them during catastrophic shocks—such as medical emergencies or structural home repairs—they are forced into the shadows. Unregulated moneylenders step into the information vacuum, offering seemingly rapid cash infusions backed by hidden compound interest and predatory land-mortgage clauses.

As illustrated in Dr. Wijewardena’s article, cases like Alice’s—where a modest Rs. 400,000 emergency loan was weaponised through legal technicalities to threaten generational land valued at Rs. 10,000,000—the absence of grassroots financial literacy transforms emergency borrowing into a mechanism of permanent class subjugation.

Conclusion: Sorting bulky operational luggage

Dr. Wijewardena’s column in the Daily FT rightly challenges us to question the stubbornness of numerical financial inclusion. But to solve the crisis, we must heed ground-level truths.

The path forward requires sorting through decades of bulky operational luggage:

Closing the 5km Gap and forcing commercial banks to extend genuine, low-barrier outreach into unbanked pockets rather than chasing safe ribbon-development corridors. Expand a shared ATM/CDM network with modern capabilities.

Taming the Shadow Debt and enforcing rigorous regulatory oversight over the Rs. 20 billion micro-debt ecosystem and protecting vulnerable families from predatory lenders. CBSL must take leadership and step into action with stakeholders.

Bridging the ICT Divide and deploying grassroots, accessible digital literacy and anti-scam awareness campaigns that protect both dropouts and qualified senior citizens alike. Open School Banking Units and Finance Society forums across the board including Senior Citizens.

Until financial literacy precedes financial inclusion—and until the State provides robust legal shields against predatory asset-stripping—the gates of the formal financial system will remain a fortress that excludes the needy while facilitating the schemer.

title: Beyond grievance: Building avenues for coexistence | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 17 October 2026 00:00
-     - 14

The Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka’s October 2026 report on the Northern and Eastern Provinces records specific, long-standing problems (The Human Rights Situation of the Northern and Eastern Provinces of Sri Lanka). Its sections on the 1990 expulsion of Northern Muslims and on freedom of religion or belief have attracted attention. The report documents the LTTE’s forced eviction of roughly 75,000 Muslims, the enduring effects of that displacement, barriers to return and secure tenure, and instances of selective administrative practice. These findings warrant serious examination. They do not constitute a communal victory. Their value lies in the practical avenues they open for peaceful coexistence, provided the Government demonstrates the will to support them.

Limits of communal victory narratives

Official recognition of past wrongs is not political vindication. The report catalogues particular failures and recommends concrete steps. It does not establish that one community’s losses were unique in kind, nor does it erase harms suffered by others. Framing the document as a long-overdue triumph for any single group risks converting an administrative process into another round of competitive grievance. Such framing also tends to confirm existing suspicions that the return of Northern Muslims is viewed by some local officials as a threat rather than as the exercise of a legal right. A more constructive reading treats the findings as an opportunity to open better avenues for shared security of tenure, equal access to services, and ordinary neighbourly relations.

Historical circumstances and shared accountability

The politics of the late 1980s and early 1990s were constrained and violent. The LTTE sought a mono-ethnic North and employed mass expulsion to advance that objective. The State confronted an insurgency that had demonstrated both military capacity and willingness to attack civilians. Local populations lived under successive occupations, shortages, and fear. These conditions help explain why certain decisions were taken; they do not render those decisions immune from later examination. Understanding context is necessary if the country is to avoid simplified moral narratives that assign permanent roles of pure victim and pure perpetrator. Parallel gaps exist in the investigation of enforced disappearances, the return of military-occupied land, and the consistent enforcement of court orders. Selective attention to one set of gaps while ignoring others would undermine the credibility of any remedial process and close rather than open avenues for coexistence.

National interest and practical avenues

Sri Lanka’s practical interest lies in treating the identified problems as national rather than communal. Land-title insecurity, missing documentation, selective application of circulars, and prolonged occupation of private land affect residents of different ethnic and religious backgrounds. The institutions capable of regularising ownership for Northern Muslim families in Puttalam, or of facilitating the return of those who wish to go back to their original districts, are the same institutions that can resolve overlapping claims involving Tamil and Sinhalese residents. A resettlement and documentation program designed for one displaced population can be structured so that it does not generate fresh grievances among others who have waited equally long. Shared economic activities—fisheries, agriculture, markets, and local infrastructure—offer further practical avenues. When communities work together on irrigation, disaster recovery, or school facilities, the incentive to maintain exclusive historical claims diminishes.

Equal treatment in practice

Equal treatment requires consistent application of existing rules rather than new communal preferences. On land, the Government can publish a time-bound program to regularise ownership of State land occupied by long-displaced families, apply identical documentary standards regardless of ethnicity or religion, and discipline officials who delay transfers on discriminatory grounds. On religion, it can issue a clear circular confirming that existing rules do not prohibit religious attire provided identification requirements are met, standardise procedures for places of worship, and enforce court orders on contested sites. On employment, public vacancies and promotion criteria in the North and East should be published with uniform tests and language requirements matched to the actual needs of the post; recruitment audits should identify and correct patterns of exclusion; and vocational training should be open to all, with placement data monitored for fairness. These steps—transparent criteria, fixed timelines, public reporting, and disciplinary follow-through—rely on existing law and administrative authority. Their implementation would reduce perceptions of selective justice and open better avenues for coexistence.

Changed climate and choice of coexistence

The post-war environment differs markedly from the years of active conflict. Open hostilities have ended. Large-scale displacement is no longer driven by combat. Economic pressures, disaster recovery, and ordinary livelihood demands occupy more public attention than wartime narratives. Political leadership has changed. Institutions such as the Human Rights Commission, the Office for Reparations, and the Office for National Unity and Reconciliation continue to operate and have, in some cases, engaged directly with affected communities. These shifts create space for peaceful coexistence that did not exist during the war. Political forgiveness need not mean forgetting specific facts. It can mean accepting that many who made decisions under wartime conditions are no longer in authority, and that future security and prosperity depend on shared rules rather than permanent moral hierarchies. It can also mean rebuilding practical relations among communities that once lived as neighbours.

Government’s will to support better avenues

The State retains the central responsibility. Existing constitutional provisions on equality, freedom of religion, and property, together with ordinary land, labour, and administrative law, are sufficient for most of the concrete problems identified. What has been missing is consistent application and visible political will. Regularising ownership of State land, enforcing existing court orders, reviewing circulars that produce discriminatory effects, withdrawing military economic activity from civilian sectors, and applying uniform recruitment standards do not require new foundational legislation. A narrowly focused inquiry into the 1990 expulsion can supply the missing official recognition without reopening every wartime controversy. The Government can demonstrate its will by issuing a single public directive that restates the principle of equal treatment, sets timelines, allocates modest resources for documentation and training, and requires periodic public reporting. Such actions would signal that the State supports avenues for coexistence and treats all residents of the North and East as equal Sri Lankan citizens.

Managing external pressures through domestic progress

Geopolitical commentary on Sri Lanka’s human rights record, land questions, and minority issues continues. Such pressures are more manageable when domestic institutions demonstrate that they can examine past events, apply existing law without systematic favouritism, and deliver tangible improvements in property security, service delivery, and employment opportunity. International statements lose force when local processes produce visible results. Managing the external dimension therefore depends less on rhetorical resistance than on the steady functioning of domestic remedies and the Government’s visible support for practical avenues of coexistence.

Conclusion

The HRCSL report records real problems. It does not declare winners. Its lasting value will depend on whether it opens better avenues for peaceful coexistence and whether the Government shows the will to support them. Secure tenure, consistent administration, equal access to employment and services, and shared economic activity under existing law offer practical paths forward. The climate has changed. The remaining question is whether institutions and communities are prepared to use that change to live together as Sri Lankans under shared rules rather than as permanent adversaries in an unfinished conflict. 

(This analysis is offered in the interest of national security, institutional reform, and public safety. The writer is a retired Senior Superintendent of Police, former head of the counter terrorism desk at the State Intelligence Service, a former member of the Sri Lanka Wakfs Board, and the author of Security Beyond Enforcement: Practical Approaches for a Safer Nation (2026).
