title: The German connection:  Why Sri Lanka needs it – and vice versa | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 17 October 2026 00:00
-     - 18

German cooperation extended into infrastructure and development, including projects associated with the Embilipitiya paper mill, the Randenigala (pictured) and Rantambe dams, the Sapugaskanda power project and sundry water-supply schemes

German trains, as opposed to Sri Lankan ones, are expected to arrive and depart when the timetable says they will

Germany can help Sri Lanka turn its latent potential into a performance befitting a nation of its lineage and heritage. Sri Lanka can remind even a European powerhouse such as Germany that performance alone is not the same thing as peace and purpose. Between the German ‘pünktlichtkeit’ (punctuality) and the Sri Lankan latitude (“pramaada-vee daavanaya-vey”) lies not merely a cultural joke, but the possibility of a genuinely reciprocal partnership. Perhaps our shared future lies somewhere between the punctual train and the late piece?

A few days after German Unity Day, it is still not late (island-style) to reflect on the nexus between the Federal Republic of Germany and the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka. 

It is late in terms of the date (3 October), yet remains timely to consider the thesis that our two countries – though they may have nothing in common as regards their national characters – are connected in an interesting enough way.

And some irony: there is, after all, an apparent absurdity in placing Sri Lanka and Germany together. More appropriate would be a felicitous (if somewhat forced) juxtaposition. 

Take Sri Lanka, at least in the uncharitable caricature of some of us, which is a country often characterised by latitude, lateness and lethargy. Time is flexible and negotiable, improvisation is a national survival skill to bolster our natural resilience, personal relationships can detour around procedures, and an appointment scheduled for nine o’clock may be understood as starting at some point in the general vicinity of noon…

Germany to my mind represents almost the opposite cultural ideal of precision, punctuality and productivity. It proactively plans, calibrates and measures, duly standardises, diligently engineers, painstakingly documents and then flawlessly executes. A German train, as opposed to a Sri Lankan one, is expected to arrive and depart when the timetable says it will. Now don’t throw current Deutsche Bahn (DB) stats at me – they used to, in my long-ago time there, at least! 

Yet, this apparent incompatibility conceals a rather important truth or a reality that is rarely if ever grasped. Sri Lanka and Germany are not natural partners because they are alike. They are somehow connected, rather, because they are so obviously different. 

Germany possesses many of the institutional, technological and supremely industrial capabilities Sri Lanka needs to strengthen. Sri Lanka harbours geographical, human, cultural and civilisational assets that Germany increasingly seeks in a bewilderingly VUCA world. Their differences are therefore not an obstacle to cooperation. They are the basis of it.

Sri Lanka and Germany do not need to be even remotely alike each other to be natural partners. They do need, however, to be reasonably complementary. Indeed, their differences may be precisely what make the unlikely partnership even more valuable.

The Federal Republic possesses many of the things Sri Lanka needs to strengthen: technological capability, industrial know-how, vocational expertise, institutional discipline, engineering excellence, substantial capital and easy access to sophisticated markets.

Be that as it may, Germany’s bilateral investment portfolio in Sri Lanka is not massive by any means. Germany Trade and Invest reports a modest if marginally enlarging footprint of $ 189 million (2022), $ 222 million (2023) and $ 243 million (2024) in terms of the Federal Republic’s FDI stock in Sri Lanka.

Our island-nation on the other hand is a repository of many things that Germany may increasingly value: An educated and adaptable population, a strategically located position in the Indian Ocean, a base from which to secure access to South Asian and Indian Ocean markets, maritime potential, abundant biodiversity and sublime cultural depth. 

There is also a marvellous if mercurial hospitality offering, whereby despite the challenges (war/tsunami/political upheaval) over the years, tourism is a great example of German-Sri Lankan reciprocity. 

Also a kaleidoscope of human talent, and an ancient civilisation struggling to coexist with plurality and uncertainty, as well as live (not always peacefully, to be honest) a peculiar island-life shaped by layers of ethnic, religious and cultural interaction…

Therefore, my proposition is not that Sri Lanka should become more German. Nor that Germany should somehow become more Sri Lankan. It is that each country can supply some of what the other seems to lack. That is the real pivot of the relationship between our republics. And interestingly, it is a nexus that has been unfolding for more than a century.

A relationship that predates diplomacy

Sri Lanka has maintained diplomatic relations with the Federal Republic of Germany (FDR), or the former West Germany, since 1953; and with East Germany – the former German Democratic Republic (DDR) – since 1970. The relationship has survived the Cold War, the division and reunification of Germany, Sri Lanka’s civil war and our beleaguered land’s recent political turmoil and economic crisis. German cooperation today encompasses vocational education, health, climate adaptation, environmental protection, reconciliation, social cohesion and maritime security. 

But the soul or intellectual connection between the two nation states goes back considerably further. Long before the modern Federal Republic’s development agencies arrived in Colombo, German scholars were travelling to Ceylon to study its language, history and religious traditions.

Wilhelm Geiger, one of the foremost German scholars of Pali and Sinhala, first came to Ceylon in 1895. He visited twice more (in 1925/6 and 1931/2), and subsequently made major contributions to the study of Sinhala, Pali and the Mahavamsa chronicle, becoming one of the most important European authorities on our blessed isle’s linguistic and historical traditions. 

And then there is Hermann Hesse. He travelled through South Asia in 1911, including Ceylon. Hesse’s encounter with the East became part of a much larger European fascination with Indian and Buddhist thought. The Goethe-Institut notes that this engagement was connected partly to a European search for something that modern industrial civilisation appeared to have lost: spirituality, wholeness, and a deeper alternative understanding of human existence. And although Hesse didn’t find the spiritually pristine civilisation he was looking for, Germany’s intellectual encounter with the South Asian hemisphere profoundly shaped parts of its modern literary and philosophical imagination.

The delicious irony is almost too good to waste on dilettantes like yours truly. Sri Lanka can look to Germany for some of the machinery of modernity. Germany once looked towards South Asia for some of the answers to the problems created by modernity. That is the first clue to a deeper symbiosis.

From lofty philosophy to plebeian buses

After Sri Lanka’s independence from European colonialism, the relationship became increasingly practical. German development cooperation in Sri Lanka dates back to 1956, according to GIZ. Its most enduring symbol is perhaps the Ceylon-German Technical Training Institute (CGTTI) in Moratuwa, better known as ‘German Tech’. 

Instituted in 1959 following an agreement the previous year between Sri Lanka and West Germany, the CGTTI was originally established in Werahera, to train technicians capable of maintaining the country’s bus fleet. German personnel initially managed the institute (later, in Moratuwa, in 1974) until Sri Lankan management eventually took over in 1976. That history deserves to be read as more than a footnote, because Germany did not simply supply Sri Lanka with equipment. Rather, it helped teach Sri Lankans how to maintain, repair and operate equipment. 

And many locomotives in the Ceylon Government Railway (CGR) and now Sri Lanka Railway (SLR) ageing fleet are operational thanks to acumen supplied by the Sri Lanka German Railway Technical Training Centre at Ratmalana which helped repair, service, maintain and re-engine those machines.

The most useful foreign assistance does not create permanent dependence. Instead, it creates domestic capability. The German contribution was therefore not merely technological. Rather, it was institutional: standards, discipline, technical education, apprenticeship and a culture of maintenance.

Over the decades, German cooperation extended into infrastructure and development, including projects associated with the Embilipitiya paper mill, the Randenigala and Rantambe dams, the Sapugaskanda power project and sundry water-supply schemes. German assistance also supported SME development and post-tsunami reconstruction. 

The pattern could be instructive. Germany brought in technological and organisational capability; Sri Lanka supplied the people, locale, local knowledge and ultimately the institutions that absorbed it. That is not a one-way relationship but complementarity in action.

In terms of trade too, the relationship is no longer simply about aid. German-Sri Lankan merchandise trade is now worth well over a billion dollars annually. In 2024, German exports to Sri Lanka exceeded $ 229 million, while German imports from Sri Lanka surpassed $ 1 billion. German exports included machinery and chemical products. Sri Lankan exports entailed substantial quantities of clothing and food. In 2025, German exports to Sri Lanka increased further, to $ 257 million, while German imports from Sri Lanka also reached a new high at $ 1.216 billion. Thus the relationship is heavily asymmetric in Sri Lanka’s favour in terms of merchandise trade, as Germany is becoming a major net importer from our land. 

This is significant because it changes the psychological nature of the relationship. Sri Lanka is not merely a recipient of German assistance but also a supplier to consumers in Germany. The Federal Republic is not merely a donor but also a customer, investor, technology provider, training partner and potential gateway to European markets.

There is institutional architecture supporting this relationship too. A double-taxation agreement has been in place since FY 1982/3, an investment-protection agreement signed by bilateral treaty in 2000 has been in force since 2004, and the Sri Lanka-Germany Business Council was established in 1999. 

The challenge now is to move the relationship from trade in goods towards cooperation in capabilities. That is where the next phase could become transformative.

What Germany can give Sri Lanka

The first priority should be skills. Sri Lanka has educated people but does not always connect education effectively to employment and industrial productivity. Germany’s dual vocational education system offers an unusually relevant model because it combines classroom education with practical workplace training and employer participation. Sri Lanka should therefore be asking Germany not merely for more vocational schools, but for help in building an entire skills-to-industry ecosystem.

Training could focus on mechatronics, industrial automation, robotics, electrical engineering, refrigeration, renewable energy, precision manufacturing, medical technology, maritime engineering, logistics and industrial maintenance. The principle should be brutally simple: train people for jobs that exist, and for industries that Sri Lanka intends to build. The German Tech experience provides a historical foundation for doing precisely this.

A second opportunity is the creation of a Sri Lankan equivalent of the German Mittelstand (the SMEs and family-owned businesses which major on patient capital, technical education, export orientation, vocational training, specialist manufacturing, institutional finance and regional industrial clusters that form the core of its economy). 

Germany’s economic strength does not rest exclusively on enormous corporations. It also hinges on technically sophisticated medium-sized enterprises that dominate specialised global niches. Sri Lanka has many thousands of SMEs, but what it lacks is a sufficiently large population of small and medium-sized enterprises that have successfully travelled the road from local business to globally competitive specialist manufacturer or service provider. German-Sri Lankan cooperation could help change that.

Technology plus skills plus standards plus finance plus export-market access could turn selected Sri Lankan SMEs into internationally competitive companies. The objective should not be to make Sri Lanka a cheaper version Germany, but enhance Sri Lankan enterprises sufficiently to compete with German companies. That is a very different ambition and perhaps runs parallel to the Federal Republic’s manifold people-to-people academic infrastructure already in place. 

These are many and varied, running the gamut from sundry scholarships and academic exchanges with German universities, German-language education and research collaboration. In fact, the German Foreign Office specifically identifies the Goethe-Institut, DAAD (a two-way street with mutual traffic for study, teaching and research), GIZ, AHK, and other socio-political foundations as being active in Sri Lanka. 

The Indian Ocean equation

There is another asset Sri Lanka possesses that Germany simply cannot acquire through technology: its unique geographic positioning. Our jewel in the Indian Ocean sits astride one of the world’s great maritime arches. Germany possesses industrial technology, engineering, logistics expertise, capital and businesses with global experience. Sri Lanka harbours ports, maritime location and proximity to India as well as the wider Indian Ocean.

Put those together and possibilities extend well beyond traditional development assistance that spans a spectrum from port technology, ship repair, maritime data, other maritime services, cold-chain and digital logistics through warehousing and green shipping to renewable energy and regional distribution.

The emerging cooperation agenda already recognises this. The Sri Lankan-German Business Forum held in Colombo in 2026 placed maritime logistics, investment and infrastructure, digitalisation, and sustainability prominently on the agenda. 

This points towards a much more interesting proposition than aid. Sri Lanka could become a more significant Germany’s Indian Ocean partner than at present. That would give Germany something it cannot manufacture at home: a strategically located platform in one of the world’s most important maritime regions.

But of a necessity in any meaningful nexus, Sri Lanka must also give. This is where the equation could lose some of its equilibrium. We in the Global South often or usually or almost always ask: ‘What can Germany do for Sri Lanka?’ May I humbly submit that we should press the converse point: What does Sri Lanka bring to Germany?

First, and perhaps uniquely, its geographic location. Second, and not so far behind, its substantial talent pool.

Germany faces certain demographic challenges and needs skilled workers in a range of sectors. Sri Lanka has a wide and deep pool of educated, technically capable and English-speaking people. The two countries could therefore construct a system of managed skills mobility in which Sri Lankans train and work in Germany while retaining strong professional and commercial links with Sri Lanka.

But the objective should be circulation, not depletion. Sri Lanka should not become merely a reservoir from which Germany extracts its most capable young people. A successful model would see Sri Lankan professionals studying in Germany, working in the Federal Republic, acquiring advanced skills, establishing businesses, returning to Sri Lanka where possible, and maintaining commercial and intellectual connections between the two countries.

Third, Sri Lanka offers Germany proximity to Indian markets, preferential access to South Asia and connectivity to the Indian Ocean.

Fourth, it can offer ecological and scientific opportunities in tropical biodiversity, marine science, climate adaptation and renewable energy.

And fifth and finally, it offers something much harder to quantify: a ‘weltanschauung’, or different conception of life.

A dual crucible

Germany has developed outstanding institutional traditions for converting technical knowledge into efficient systems. Sri Lanka’s civilisational inheritance has wrestled for centuries with issues that systems alone cannot satisfy – such as suffering, impermanence, consciousness, community, spirituality, and the symbiotic relationship between human beings and nature. Neither ethos is sufficient for human happiness in and of itself, because efficiency without purpose becomes sterile and purpose without efficiency becomes impotent.

Sri Lanka’s problem, so to say, is not that it has too much humanity and too little Teutonic efficiency. Its challenge is that it has often failed to convert its considerable human and natural assets into properly functioning systems. Germany can help with that. For its part, Germany’s dilemma is not that it is too efficient; it is that no industrial society can live indefinitely by pure efficiency alone. Sri Lankan spirituality can contribute something to that too.

That is why the historical experience of Geiger, Hesse et al. matters. The German-Sri Lankan relationship began, in one sense, with Germans coming to Sri Lanka to understand one thing, and continued with Germans coming to Sri Lanka to build something else. The next phase of their mutual development could involve both countries coming together to create something neither can create alone.

The two countries have already demonstrated in some respects that such a partnership can work.

A German technical institute established to keep Sri Lankan buses running became a Sri Lankan institution. German scholars once travelled to Ceylon to study its civilisation, and enlightened a world walking in darkness at the time. 

Sri Lankan manufacturers now sell goods to German consumers. Federal Republic businesses are again examining our sun- and rain-blessed island as an Indian Ocean investment and logistics platform. And both countries are now discussing cooperation in precisely those areas where their capabilities intersect: skills, technology, maritime infrastructure, logistics, sustainability, investment and innovation. 

So even belatedly I’m suggesting that perhaps the central question is not why Germany and Sri Lanka get along despite being so different – it is whether they get along because they are so different. 

If there is any good reason why the relationship isn’t stronger or more significant than it is already, consider Sri Lanka’s notorious policy instability, weak investment predictability, regulatory friction, skills mismatch, small domestic market, infrastructure constraints, political risk, German corporate risk aversion, Sri Lanka’s comparatively limited industrial depth, strong competition from our neighbours, bureaucratic inefficiency and the lack of a comprehensive Sri Lanka-EU trade agreement…

No doubt there is room for reflection on these realities on both sides of the border, so to speak. But if the further foundation is laid well, the ultimate payoff may be surprisingly simple. Germany can help Sri Lanka turn its latent potential into a performance befitting a nation of its lineage and heritage. Sri Lanka can remind even a European powerhouse such as Germany that performance alone is not the same thing as peace and purpose.

Between the German ‘pünktlichtkeit’ (punctuality) and the Sri Lankan latitude (“pramaada-vee daavanaya-vey”) lies not merely a cultural joke, but the possibility of a genuinely reciprocal partnership. Perhaps our shared future lies somewhere between the punctual train and the late piece?

(The writer is the Editor-at-large of LMD and is a senior journalist with a Post-graduate Diploma in Politics and Governance)

title: Mahaweli Doctrine 2.0: Sri Lanka in  an age of fragmented interdependence | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 17 October 2026 00:00
-     - 15

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake (left) with the author

In an age of fragmented interdependence, Sri Lanka does not need merely to stand between great powers. It must learn to flow among them—like the Mahaweli—drawing strength from many tributaries, converting external relationships into domestic capacity, and remaining unmistakably Sri Lankan in its destination

When I introduced the “Mahaweli Doctrine” in the Daily FT in July, I argued that Sri Lanka’s foreign policy should behave like its greatest river: not divide but connect; not isolate but unite; and link villages to global markets, local enterprise to international opportunity, and ancient wisdom to modern statecraft.

That proposition has become even more urgent, especially following the Washington summit between President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping. The international system is not simply moving from American unipolarity to Chinese primacy, nor is it dividing neatly into two rival blocs. Instead, the world is entering what I call an “age of fragmented interdependence.”

Put simply, countries — including island nations like Sri Lanka — may depend on the United States for security, finance, technology, or education while depending on China for manufacturing, trade, infrastructure, and supply chains. The same country may deepen strategic relations with India, attract investment from the Gulf, trade with Europe, work with Japan on development, and seek markets in ASEAN and across the Global South.

For Sri Lanka, this is not merely a description of the world. It should become a framework for statecraft in pursuit of “economic freedom” — moving beyond a historical dependence on the World Bank, the IMF, and other external lenders toward greater national economic capacity and resilience.

The Mahaweli Doctrine must therefore evolve from nonalignment to multi-alignment, and from multi-alignment toward strategic connectivity with sovereign guardrails. The objective is neither equidistance nor opportunistic balancing. It is to connect different external partners to different national needs while preventing any single relationship from becoming a source of strategic dependence.

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake has described “economic freedom” as the unfinished business of Sri Lanka’s independence. That insight deserves to be placed at the center of foreign policy. A country that cannot finance essential imports, withstand an energy shock, protect critical infrastructure, create productive employment, or negotiate from a position of fiscal strength cannot exercise complete strategic autonomy.

Economic freedom, therefore, is not separate from national security. It is one of its foundations.

From Plymouth and Jamestown to Polonnaruwa

As a former American diplomat and professor, my reflections and writings on Sino-American relations have repeatedly taken me back to the historical origins of the United States. The American experience contained two powerful impulses almost from its beginning.

Jamestown in Virginia, founded in 1607 as a commercial venture, represented enterprise and the search for material prosperity. Plymouth in Massachusetts, founded in 1620 by the Pilgrims, represented another aspiration: religious community and freedom of conscience.

Neither story should be romanticised, and both unfolded within a larger colonial history that brought devastating consequences for Indigenous peoples. Yet, as historical archetypes, they illuminate an enduring American tension between material ambition and moral purpose—a tension that ultimately helped generate extraordinary innovation and economic dynamism.

More than a century later, Adam Smith gave intellectual expression to a similar duality.  ‘The Wealth of Nations,’ published in 1776, explained the productive power of specialisation, exchange, and commerce. But Smith had already written ‘The Theory of Moral Sentiments’ in 1759, examining sympathy, conscience, justice, and the moral foundations of human society.

Markets require trust. Wealth requires purpose. The same tension appeared in the American founding. Alexander Hamilton understood that political independence without public credit, productive capacity, commerce, and finance would leave the new republic vulnerable. Thomas Jefferson represented a republican suspicion of concentrated economic and political power.

America needed something from both: Hamiltonian capacity and Jeffersonian restraint—or, as I described it in my book ‘Trade for Peace,’ Hamiltonian means to Jeffersonian ends.

Sri Lanka has its own, much older vocabulary for this relationship. King Parakramabahu I understood that water sustained agriculture; agriculture created surplus; surplus enabled commerce; commerce connected ports and markets; commercial networks required security; and security ultimately required diplomacy. Long before Hamilton or Smith, ancient Sri Lanka demonstrated that productive capacity, international commerce, and strategic power could reinforce one another.

The genius of Sri Lanka’s hydraulic civilisation was not simply that it built reservoirs. It built systems—transforming water into agricultural abundance, agricultural abundance into commercial capacity, and commercial capacity into wider regional influence in Asia.

America and China: Two portfolios of power in fragmented interdependence

The contemporary Sino-American competition should not be reduced to the proposition that America possesses military power while China possesses economic power. The United States remains an extraordinary military, economic, technological, financial, diplomatic, and educational power. China is simultaneously an industrial, commercial, technological, and diplomatic power with rapidly expanding military capabilities.

What differs is the composition and geographical expression of their power. The United States has, for example, an unparalleled network of alliances and security partnerships, together with deep capital markets, leading universities and technology companies, and the continuing centrality of the dollar. China has developed another enormous network: manufacturing supply chains, ports, infrastructure, industrial capacity, trade relationships, and development finance.

The 2026 meetings between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping illustrate this changing relationship. The Council on Foreign Relations observed after the May Beijing summit that both governments embraced the language of “strategic stability” while attaching different meanings to it. Washington emphasised transactions and economic deliverables; Beijing gave the term broader political content involving the management of competition and respect for what it regards as its core interests.

In September, the Washington summit produced tariff reductions covering $ 30 billion in non-sensitive goods in each direction, an artificial-intelligence dialogue, a trade mechanism, and an extension of the economic truce. Yet the deeper strategic rivalry remains.

Other observers portray this changing relationship as part of Asia’s wider re-emergence and point to a Chinese perception of being strategically constrained by American alliances and deployments extending from Japan through the Philippines. That is a perspective, not an uncontested fact. Washington and its Asian allies, in turn, view Chinese military modernisation, pressure around Taiwan, and maritime behavior as sources of insecurity.

This reciprocal perception is important for Sri Lanka. Great powers increasingly interpret economics through security—and security through economics. Semiconductors, artificial intelligence, rare earths, ports, energy networks, data, shipping routes, and supply chains now belong to both domains. That is fragmented interdependence.

Sri Lanka must not become somebody else’s strategic geography

For centuries, Sri Lanka’s location attracted merchants, monks,  travellers, missionaries, imperial powers, and navies. Geography, however, is not automatically an asset. It becomes an asset only when national strategy converts location into prosperity while protecting sovereignty. Otherwise, geography becomes a liability.

The Portuguese, Dutch, and British did not come because Sri Lanka was irrelevant. They came precisely because the island was valuable to the commercial and strategic networks of their times. Contemporary policymakers should remember that lesson.

Sri Lanka should welcome Indian investment and connectivity without becoming merely an extension of Indian strategic geography. It should welcome Chinese investment without becoming an extension of Chinese strategic geography. It should deepen relations with the United States without becoming an instrument of American strategic competition. And it should cultivate Japan, Europe, ASEAN, the Middle East, Africa, and other partners without allowing excessive dependence on any single relationship to diminish its freedom of action.

This is not equidistance. Geography makes some relationships different from others, and India’s proximity gives it a unique significance. Nor is this passive neutrality. It is strategic autonomy through diversified interdependence.

The relevant question is not, “Which great power should Sri Lanka choose?” It is, “How can each relationship strengthen Sri Lanka while no relationship controls Sri Lanka?”

Mahatma Gandhi offered a remarkably appropriate metaphor for the predicament of smaller nations in an interconnected world: “I want the cultures of all lands to be blown about my house as freely as possible. But I refuse to be blown off my feet by any.”

For Sri Lanka, this should become an organising principle of fragmented interdependence: open the windows in every direction, but remain firmly rooted in our own house—built upon the foundations of the Mahaweli civilisation.

Different tributaries, one national river

The Mahaweli provides the appropriate metaphor. A river does not ask whether useful water originated in one tributary or another. Different streams enter the system, but they ultimately serve a larger national ecology. Foreign policy can operate similarly:

The objective should not be to calculate which external power receives what percentage of Sri Lanka. It should be to determine which combination of relationships best advances the national interest. In other words, every tributary should flow into the same Sri Lankan reservoir.

Five sovereign guardrails

Fragmented interdependence requires discipline. Diversification without strategy can simply create multiple dependencies. The Mahaweli Doctrine should therefore be supported by five sovereign guardrails.

First, no single external partner should acquire indispensable leverage over critical national systems. Ports, energy, telecommunications, data, transport, water, and other strategic infrastructure require transparent governance, resilience, and appropriate diversification.

Second, foreign investment should be judged primarily by national productivity rather than geopolitical identity. The central question should not be whether capital is American, Chinese, Indian, Japanese, European, or Arab. Policymakers should ask whether an investment creates productive employment, transfers technology and skills, strengthens Sri Lankan enterprises, generates exports or foreign exchange, and leaves behind durable national capacity.

Third, Sri Lanka should avoid unnecessary exclusivity in strategic commitments. A small island situated along major sea lanes derives influence from being useful and trusted by many partners rather than subordinate to one.

Fourth, economic diplomacy must reach beyond Colombo. This was central to the original Mahaweli Doctrine. Foreign policy should connect Polonnaruwa’s farmers, Jaffna’s entrepreneurs, Trincomalee’s harbor, Rajarata’s universities, Hambantota’s logistics, Colombo’s financial institutions, and enterprises in every province to global opportunity. The Grama Niladhari and district networks could help identify exportable products, investment needs, tourism assets, and skills that Sri Lankan missions and embassies abroad can connect to international markets.

Fifth, Sri Lanka must build sufficient domestic capacity to say both “yes” and “no.” Strategic autonomy is impossible without fiscal space, reserves, energy resilience, food security, institutional competence, human capital, and technological capability.

At the end of the day, sovereignty is not merely a flag. Sovereignty is national capacity—and human resource development through education is central to building that capacity.

From stabilisation to transformation

This is particularly relevant to the administration of President Dissanayake. Sri Lanka has already learned the severe consequences of the interaction between external vulnerability and domestic weakness.

There has been significant progress since the crisis. In September, the International Monetary Fund reported that gross official reserves had risen to $6.9 billion by the end of August 2026, that banks remained well capitalised and profitable, and that debt restructuring was largely completed. Earlier IMF reporting noted that public debt had declined from 125.8 percent of GDP in 2022 to 101.1 percent in 2025.

But the same IMF assessment warned that risks remain tilted to the downside because of global trade uncertainty, energy and geopolitical shocks, climate conditions, and continuing domestic vulnerabilities. Its formulation is especially relevant: Sri Lanka now needs to move from “stabilisation to transformation.”

That transformation should become the economic dimension of the Mahaweli Doctrine. Stabilisation prevents collapse. Transformation creates capacity.

The next stage must therefore emphasise export diversification, productive investment, human capital, digital capability, energy resilience, competitive enterprises, effective institutions, and adequate external buffers. President Dissanayake’s concept of economic freedom can supply the political purpose: macroeconomic indicators matter, but they become meaningful when they enlarge the real choices available to citizens and the strategic choices available to the State.

Here again, the reservoir provides a useful analogy. A reservoir is valuable not merely because water enters it. Water must be stored, managed, distributed, and transformed into productive activity.

Foreign capital should be treated in much the same way. Sri Lanka should not celebrate investment merely because money arrives. Policymakers should ask: Where does it flow? What does it produce? Whom does it employ? What knowledge does it transfer? What foreign exchange does it generate? What environmental costs does it impose? And what national capability remains after the investor receives a legitimate return?

That is the difference between attracting capital and achieving development.

From nonalignment, through multi-alignment, to strategic connectivity

Sri Lanka has a distinguished tradition in the Non-Aligned Movement, and the Dissanayake administration continues to describe its foreign policy as non-aligned. That principle remains valuable. But classical nonalignment emerged in a different international system.

Today, the challenge is not simply to remain outside military blocs. It is to participate simultaneously in overlapping economic, technological, financial, security, and diplomatic networks without surrendering national autonomy.

The progression should therefore be understood as: Nonalignment → Multi-alignment → Strategic Connectivity. Here, nonalignment protects independence of judgment; multi-alignment diversifies partnerships; strategic connectivity converts those partnerships into national capability.

This final step is crucial. Diplomacy should be measured not by the number of high-level visits, memoranda, or photographs, but by whether those relationships increase Sri Lanka’s productive capacity and resilience. A foreign-policy meeting should ultimately connect to a factory, university, port, farm, technology transfer, export contract, tourism flow, research partnership, or skilled job somewhere on the island.

Grand Central Station of the Indian Ocean

I have previously described Sri Lanka as a potential “Grand Central Station” of commerce, culture, and spirituality in the Indian Ocean.

A great station does not choose only one train. Its importance derives from the number of destinations it connects. Colombo, Hambantota, Trincomalee, Jaffna, Galle, and Sri Lanka’s emerging economic corridors should therefore not become geopolitical trophies conceptually belonging to one external power or another. They should become Sri Lankan nodes connecting South Asia, Southeast Asia, East Asia, the Middle East, Africa, Europe, and the Americas.

The same principle should extend beyond ports. Sri Lanka can become a meeting place for finance, logistics, higher education, digital services, maritime activity, tourism, culture, and interfaith exchange.

This would transform the island from an object of great-power competition into a platform for international cooperation. In a fragmented world, connectivity itself can become a form of power.

The lesson of Parakramabahu: The power of diplomacy

Nearly nine centuries ago, King Parakramabahu I did not possess the vocabulary of geoeconomics, strategic autonomy, multi-alignment, or fragmented interdependence. He understood something more elemental that national power begins with productive capacity. It requires infrastructure. Infrastructure enables commerce. Commerce requires connectivity. Connectivity requires security. And sustainable security ultimately depends upon diplomacy.

That is why the Mahaweli Doctrine is not simply a foreign policy metaphor. It is simultaneously a development doctrine and a national security doctrine.

The emerging world does not require Sri Lanka to choose Washington over Beijing, Beijing over Washington, India over China, or China over India. Nor should Sri Lanka assume that great powers will organise their policies around our interests. They will pursue their own. Our responsibility is to pursue ours.

The island should welcome many tributaries of investment, technology, knowledge, security cooperation, and commerce, but it must build institutions capable of directing those flows toward a common national purpose.

America’s historical experience teaches that wealth and values, markets and institutions, capacity and restraint must be held together. China’s rise demonstrates the strategic power of production, infrastructure, trade, and long-term economic connectivity. Sri Lanka’s own hydraulic civilisation teaches an even older lesson: resources become power only when they are intelligently connected—and, for that, capable diplomacy is indispensable.

President Dissanayake has spoken of completing Sri Lanka’s independence through economic freedom. The Mahaweli Doctrine offers one way to translate that aspiration into external strategy through diplomacy.

In an age of fragmented interdependence, Sri Lanka does not need merely to stand between great powers. It must learn to flow among them—like the Mahaweli—drawing strength from many tributaries, converting external relationships into domestic capacity, and remaining unmistakably Sri Lankan in its destination.

(The author is a former US diplomat and military professor at NATO and the US Indo-Pacific Command, has worked at the World Bank and the United Nations. The first Sri Lankan Youth Ambassador to the United Nations in New York, Prof. Mendis has established scholarships and awards at the University of Sri Jayewardenepura, Rajarata University of Sri Lanka, the University of Minnesota, and Harvard University. He is a Distinguished Visiting Professor of Transatlantic Relations at the University of Warsaw and resides in Poland and Washington, D.C., United States)

title: Rooftop solar with battery storage: Significant growth potential not recognised | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 17 October 2026 00:00
-     - 18

I have been following the recent grid connected rooftop solar PV conundrum posted on social media and feel compelled to respond. 

The State technocrats have been slow to adapt to the rapid developments taking place in the business of rooftop harnessing of solar. The term ‘disruptive technology’ is not new. However, the disruption today is supercharged, and national policy makers with conventional mindsets seem to be overwhelmed. They appear to lack vision, the ability to think out of the box and may be handicapped by the prevailing bureaucratic culture and outdated processes. 

Rooftop solar aligns closely with the national goal of renewable energy dominance to be attained over the coming decades. This sector also aligns development goals such as energy security, technological advancement, avenues for investment, skilled job creation, etc. with investment and job creation spread nationwide.

The experience gained from the Sri Lanka Sooriya Bala program launched in 2016 (enhance renewable energy generation), continuing installations with lessons learned, emergence of new ideas and resulting debates, the experiences overseas (specially Australia) and the Solar Industries Association recommendations made recently to the PUCSL (Long Term Power System Development Plan) represents a significant resource of operational experiences and creative ideas for moving the rooftop solar program further forward rapidly. 

This effort is aided with falling costs of solar PV, and battery energy system storage systems (BESS) and technological advancements. Thus, the scale up potential for rooftop solar applications is significant. 

The prosumer 

Prosumers are consumers of electricity who also produce their own electricity at the point of consumption (most commonly via rooftop solar). They can also handle their own electricity production by using BESS for storing and later consumption or for exporting electricity to the grid. The regulatory policies that facilitate the emergence of the prosumers already exist in Sri Lanka with Net Metering, Net Accounting, Net Plus and Net Plus Plus with these offering different commercial arrangements. These must be adapted to encourage storage, controllability and grid-support services rather than simply maximising uncontrolled solar exports. Unfortunately, while prosumer growth is on an upward trend, there are signs that the State technocrats seek to slow down or curtail this promising sector due challenges faced on the grid management front.

Prosumers can emerge from the electricity consumer categories such as residential, commercial, industrial, military facility, hospital, campus, etc. and operate as a micro utility (networked or isolated). 

They could be subject to a market rate tariff (time of use) and daily peak demand charge. Additionally, they can be financially incentivised to sign up for a Demand Side Management (DSM) program where they volunteer to reduce grid imports, shift load, discharge batteries, limit charging, or - where technically and commercially permitted - export power. The prosumer can utilise smart controls aided with AI (if useful) to optimise benefits. 

We now have in place an element of the national power system that incorporates distributed generation and storage of electricity at scale. The system will be smart, integrated and network centric. 

The National System Operator (NSO) and Regional Electricity Companies (RECs) will utilise smart energy-management systems, increasingly incorporating AI-based forecasting and optimisation. The NSO and RECs would use load forecasts, weather forecasts, real-time measurements, and distributed-resource data to estimate regional and national demand and the expected output of distributed solar resources.

Challenge of controlling a distributed system

Distributed system visibility is an important factor that needs to be addressed. How can the NSO and RECs effectively dispatch thousands of prosumer BESS individually? 

Inverter-based BESS can do considerably more than shift solar energy. They can potentially provide numerous services such as peak shaving and demand response, voltage/reactive-power support, frequency-response services, etc.

Thousands of 5-100 kW resources are individually insignificant to the NSO. Aggregated, they could represent hundreds of MW. How can they be utilised effectively as virtual power plants? The technical aspects of control, operation management, and optimised operation of a networked system of prosumers need to be studied. Additionally, the commercial and legal aspects that arise when promoting rapid growth of the prosumer business should be addressed.

Consumers to prosumers

High consumption electricity consumers (affluent demographic) will most likely transform into prosumers when electricity is sold at market rate. A variable tariff with smart meter and peak demand charge will coax the consumer to install grid connected rooftop solar with battery storage and smart devices for controlling load.

Incentives such as duty-free imports and tax rebates should be offered to new entry prosumers since the nation benefits significantly from the energy and technology fronts. 

The prosumer’s investment converts the indigenous and freely available solar resource into electricity at the point of consumption, reducing dependence on imported fuels and avoiding part of the transmission and distribution burden associated with centrally generated electricity.

Affordable or market rate electricity tariff

The term “affordable electricity” should not apply to the groups identified. Service and industrial sectors that are vital to the national economy and unable to exploit solar energy for joining the ranks of the prosumers should be compensated via creative fiscal arrangements. Poorer segments of society should not be exempted from a market rate tariff. This will help to increase awareness among citizens and reduce waste and possible ‘electricity theft’. Where the Government wishes to protect vulnerable households, targeted social assistance could be considered as an alternative to broadly suppressing electricity price signals. The use of a State-controlled electricity sector to dispense social welfare is an outdated concept.

Prosumers aiding the renewable-energy transition

The prosumer model could become an important element of Sri Lanka’s renewable-energy transition, alongside utility-scale solar and wind. Its greatest value is not simply adding more rooftop PV; it is creating thousands of distributed, controllable solar + BESS resources that can absorb surplus daytime solar, reduce evening peak demand, provide demand response, and eventually act collectively as a virtual power plant.

What is described above is not rocket science. The industry is mature and operational at numerous locations worldwide and many industry professionals have presented papers that cover the technical and commercial aspects of the prosumer business thriving in a smart grid environment.

Sri Lanka is not short of talent for mastering the technology and promoting this sector at scale. The Universities of Moratuwa and Peradeniya operate stateoftheart microgrid systems.

The University of Moratuwa/LECO microgrid features 350 kW of solar PV, a 400 kWh BESS and a 630 kVA backup diesel generator, with remote load control and islanding capability.

The University of Peradeniya microgrid features a 60 kW hybrid inverter, 100 kWh BESS integrated with its existing 60 kW solar PV installation. The university describes this as an advanced AC microgrid supporting computer servers and its developing AI laboratory.

University academics have made presentations in the recent past that covered renewable energy penetration, distributed generation, and the emergence of prosumers. The Solar Industries Association has also presented a policy paper that describes this application.

Unfortunately, while the CEB acknowledges the multiple challenges faced with rooftop solar such as distribution-level voltage constraints, with poor observability of distributed solar, midday surplus generation, etc. the prosumer idea has not spread far. This phenomenon is most likely due to docile advocacy and conventional thinking of State sector technocrats who act as reluctant elements rather than enthusiastic advocates excited by technological developments taking place in the rooftop solar and BESS fronts.

While mastering and rapidly developing this vital sector shows signs of lethargy,  

technical universities will continue to offer subsidised engineering education to our youth for meeting the skilled human resource needs of the rapidly growing global renewable energy industry.

Thrice beaten Bangladesh saved their best performance for the last when they gave Sri Lanka a close run in the final of the Pakistan Women’s Under19 T20 Tri-Series before losing by four runs in a thrilling contest at the Iqbal Stadium in Faisalabad yesterday.

Bangladesh who were bowled out for 58 in their last league game against Sri Lanka, took up the challenge of chasing 159 for victory and finished eventually on 154-7 with Sri Lanka holding onto their nerve in a tight finish.

Bangladesh required 19 off the final over bowled by off-spinner Chamodhi Herath and they nearly made it with Sadia Akter (35 off 22 balls, 1 four, 3 sixes) getting them close to the line before succumbing to a brilliant diving catch in the deep by Shashini Gimhani off the penultimate ball of the match with Bangladesh needing 9 runs. The final ball was hit for four, but Sri Lanka already had the match in the bag.

Bangladesh got off to the worst start losing both openers without scoring to be 4-2 in 2 overs. They lost a third wicket at 21, but a fourth wicket stand of 67 off 51 balls between Nishita Akter (32 off 33) and skipper Sadia Islam put them back on track. Islam kept her team in the hunt racing to a stroke-filled half-century (59 off 36 balls, 3 fours, 5 sixes) but fell with the score at 109, leaving Sadia Akter to carry the fight to the Lankans.

Earlier Sri Lanka put into bat first reached a challenging score of 158-6 with their in-form opening batter Sanjana Kavindi scoring her third fifty of the Tri-Series – a hard hit 64 off 44 balls (7 fours, 2 sixes) reaching her half-century off 35 balls with a six.

Kavindi shared an opening stand of 49 in 5 overs with Vimoksha Balasuriya (23) and 55 off 46 balls for the second wicket with Nethmi Upeksha (22). Sri Lanka lost a few cheap wickets but Umayangana Peiris (28* off 23) ensured they ended up with a total which was to be the highest made in the Tri-Series.  

Sanjana Kavindi bagged both individual awards that were on offer taking the Player of the Final for her knock of 64 and Player of the Series award for accumulating 316 runs (avg. 63.20) with 3 fifties and a strike rate of 138. (ST)
